Hi Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo today. It was helpful to see Redwood's autoscaling and warm-pool behavior. A quick recap of our high-level targets we discussed so your team can start sizing:

- p95 latency (streaming): <= 200ms
- Sustained throughput target: ~500 req/s
- Typical concurrency: 30–50 concurrent streams
- Burst capacity: up to 200–250 req/s for short spikes (~1–2 minutes)
- Queueing tolerance: up to ~5s for non-interactive calls; streaming interactions need <500ms end-to-end

A few open questions we promised to confirm:
1) How long does a cold scale-up typically take to hit burst concurrency targets?
2) Does Redwood support a warm pool to avoid cold starts for streaming contexts? If so, what are warm-pool sizing best practices?
3) How does request queueing interact with SLOs — is there automatic shedding or prioritized routing?

Can your team share a simple worksheet or config recommendation for mapping these targets to an autoscaling policy? Happy to book a follow-up next week.

Thanks,

Hi Sophie —

Great to meet you and the FinEdge team. Appreciate the clear targets; that helps a lot. Attaching an SLO worksheet and our performance whitepaper — the worksheet maps p95 latency and target throughput to recommended instance pools, warm-pool sizes, and expected scale-up timelines.

Quick answers / clarifications from our side:
- Cold scale-up: Depends on model variant and instance type. For our typical LLM configs, cold-to-ready (accepting traffic) is ~12–30s; for some larger quantized models it can be 45–90s.
- Warm pools: Yes — we recommend keeping a small warm pool to meet streaming p95 targets. For your target of p95<=200ms with 30–50 concurrency, a warm pool sized for ~20% of baseline concurrency usually hits most bursts without queuing.
- Autoscale policy behavior: Redwood supports both reactive autoscaling (CPU/GPU utilization + queue depth) and proactive warm-pool triggers. Queueing is exposed in metrics; you can configure max queue wait and automatic shedding for best-effort traffic. Critical streaming requests can be prioritized and routed to warm-pool instances to avoid queueing.

Proposed next steps:
1) Fill out the attached SLO_worksheet.xlsx with a typical traffic profile (peak/min/percentile bursts).
2) We'll run a quick sizing calc and propose a Dedicated config + warm-pool recommendation and expected cost delta.
3) 30-minute technical follow-up (we can do next Wed or Thu) to walk the proposed config and trade-offs.

Attachments:
- SLO_worksheet.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)
- redwood-inference-performance-whitepaper.pdf (application/pdf)

Cheers,

Sophie / team —

Adding some technical detail so you have concrete knobs to consider when you fill the worksheet:

- Warm pool sizing: assume each warm replica can support ~3–5 concurrent streaming requests with p95<=200ms (depends on model/quant). For your 30–50 concurrency baseline, start with 10 warm replicas (assuming 5 conc per replica) and tune from there.
- Burst handling: for 200–250 req/s short spikes, combine warm-pool capacity with short-term autoscale ramp (scale-up policy to add nodes within 20–45s) plus a small request queue (max wait 3–5s). The queue should only be used for best-effort requests; critical streaming traffic gets priority and is sent to warm replicas.
- Cold start caveat: if you rely on pure reactive cold starts (no warm pool), expect degraded p95 during the 30–90s window. For SLAs that require tight p95 targets we strongly recommend designated warm capacity for the critical routes.

Operational suggestions:
- Route types: split interactive streaming routes (low latency + priority) from batch/async routes (higher queue tolerance).
- Monitoring: expose queue depth and warm-pool utilization as SLO indicators; trigger alerts at 60–70% warm utilization.

Happy to walk through a worked example if you want — I can take the numbers from the SLO worksheet and return a suggested Dedicated config + cost impact.

— Rishi
Lead Systems Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
